title: Cortical and modified radical mastoidectomy
subtitle: Find the lateral canal, then you know where the nerve is

sources.org: European Academy of Otology and Neurotology and Japan Otological Society (EAONO/JOS)
sources.title: EAONO/JOS joint consensus statements on the definitions, classification and staging of middle ear cholesteatoma (Yung M et al., J Int Adv Otol)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Otitis media with effusion in under 12s (NG233)

indications: Cortical (simple, canal wall up) mastoidectomy: acute mastoiditis not responding to intravenous antibiotics, a subperiosteal abscess, coalescent mastoiditis, or an otogenic intracranial complication, together with the appropriate team.
Cortical mastoidectomy as part of other surgery: chronic mucosal disease with tympanoplasty, or access for cochlear implantation.

Modified radical (canal wall down) mastoidectomy: cholesteatoma that cannot be reliably removed with the canal wall intact, for example extensive disease in a sclerotic mastoid, a destroyed posterior canal wall, a lateral canal fistula, or a patient unlikely to attend for second-look surgery or imaging surveillance.
Revision of a failed canal wall up procedure with recurrent or residual cholesteatoma.
contraindications: Medical unfitness for a long general anaesthetic, where aural toilet and imaging surveillance may be the safer choice for limited cholesteatoma.
Disease in an only hearing ear is a relative contraindication. The decision is made by an experienced otologist with the patient fully informed.
Uncorrected coagulopathy, except in a life-threatening complication of acute mastoiditis where the risk of not operating is greater.
Intracranial complications with raised pressure are managed with the neurosurgical team first; the ear is drained as part of a joint plan, not in isolation.
preparation: High-resolution CT of the temporal bones on screen in theatre, reviewed for the tegmen height, the position of the sigmoid sinus, mastoid pneumatisation, a dehiscent facial canal, a lateral canal fistula and the extent of disease. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging where residual or intracranial disease is suspected.
Pure tone audiogram of both ears within an agreed interval, with masking, so any post-operative hearing change can be measured. Tuning fork tests confirm it on the day.
Document facial nerve function before surgery with a recognised scale.

Consent risks to discuss: facial nerve weakness, temporary or permanent; hearing loss including a dead ear; tinnitus; vertigo and imbalance; taste disturbance from chorda tympani injury; cerebrospinal fluid leak; residual or recurrent cholesteatoma and further surgery; a mastoid cavity that needs lifelong cleaning and may discharge; numbness of the pinna; and wound infection.
For acute mastoiditis, send blood cultures before antibiotics where possible and image for intracranial complications if the child or adult is not improving.
positioning: Supine with the head turned away from the operative ear on a head ring, the mastoid uppermost. Check the neck is not over-rotated, particularly in older patients.
Head-up tilt and the table rotated as needed so the surgeon can see down the canal without the patient's head being moved.
Face visible under clear drapes if facial nerve monitoring is used.
Pressure care for a long operation: heels, sacrum and the dependent ear.
equipment: Operating microscope with an otological objective, and an otological drill with cutting and diamond burrs of a full range of sizes, continuous suction-irrigation.
Otological microinstruments: Rosen needle, round knife, Plester or similar elevators, House curettes, alligator forceps, Bellucci scissors, and fine suckers of several sizes.
Temporalis fascia press, gelatin sponge, bone wax, oxidised cellulose, and ribbon gauze with bismuth iodoform paraffin paste or an alternative ear pack.
anatomy: The suprameatal (Macewen's) triangle, bounded by the temporal line above, the posterosuperior canal wall in front and a tangent behind, overlies the mastoid antrum, which lies roughly 1.5 cm deep in the adult and much closer to the surface in an infant.
The tegmen (middle fossa dura) forms the roof, and the sigmoid sinus the posterior boundary. A low tegmen or anterior sigmoid sinus, seen on CT, narrows the safe working space.
Koerner's septum (the petrosquamous lamina) can be mistaken for the medial wall of the antrum. The antrum lies deep to it.

The lateral semicircular canal is the key landmark: a smooth, dense, yellowish prominence in the floor of the aditus. The tympanic segment of the facial nerve lies just below and in front of it, and the second genu just below its anterior end.

The mastoid (vertical) segment of the facial nerve runs from the second genu down to the stylomastoid foramen, deep to the posterior canal wall, in the facial ridge. The chorda tympani leaves it to run forwards.
In a canal wall down operation the posterior canal wall is lowered to the level of the facial nerve, and the cavity, middle ear and canal become one space opened by a meatoplasty.
criticalSafety: Identify the lateral semicircular canal before working anywhere near the facial nerve, and use it to locate the nerve.
Identify the tegmen and the sigmoid sinus early and follow them, so the cavity has known boundaries.
Lower the facial ridge with a diamond burr, parallel to the nerve, with irrigation, until the nerve is seen through thin bone. Do not expose it unnecessarily.
Never pull cholesteatoma matrix off the stapes or off a suspected lateral canal fistula. Leave it, or remove it last and deliberately, with senior input.
Stop drilling near the ossicles if the burr could touch them.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve: tympanic segment, second genu, mastoid segment
Lateral semicircular canal and inner ear (fistula, dead ear)
Middle fossa dura and tegmen (cerebrospinal fluid leak, brain herniation)
Sigmoid sinus and jugular bulb (haemorrhage, air embolism)
commonErrors: Drilling a narrow, deep hole towards the antrum instead of saucerising, so landmarks are lost and the depth cannot be seen.
Mistaking Koerner's septum for the medial wall and believing the antrum has been reached.
A high facial ridge left in a canal wall down cavity, which traps debris and causes a chronically discharging cavity.
An inadequate meatoplasty, so the cavity cannot be seen or cleaned in clinic.
Missing disease in the sinus tympani, anterior epitympanum or around the stapes.
complications: Facial nerve palsy, immediate or delayed.
Sensorineural hearing loss, including a dead ear, and vertigo, particularly with a lateral canal fistula or ossicular trauma.
Cerebrospinal fluid leak or brain herniation through a tegmen defect; bleeding from the sigmoid sinus or a high jugular bulb.
Residual or recurrent cholesteatoma, a discharging cavity, meatal stenosis, perichondritis of the pinna, wound infection and taste disturbance.
postop: Document facial function in recovery. Check for nystagmus and vertigo and perform tuning fork tests once awake.
Head bandage and ear pack as per surgeon's practice; the pack is usually removed in clinic after one to three weeks.
Keep the ear dry. Avoid nose blowing and straining in the early weeks.
A canal wall down cavity needs periodic clinic cleaning for life. After a canal wall up procedure, plan a second look or diffusion-weighted MRI surveillance for residual cholesteatoma.
Post-operative audiogram once the ear has healed.

steps.emphasis: Confirm consent covers the possible conversion from canal wall up to canal wall down, and ossicular reconstruction or a staged procedure.
Temporal bone CT on screen and the audiogram. Read aloud the side, the tegmen height, the sigmoid position and any fistula or facial canal dehiscence.
Antibiotic per local policy and any culture results; in acute mastoiditis the patient is already on treatment and pus is sent from the cavity.
Head turned away, mastoid uppermost, without over-rotating the neck. Face visible for monitoring.
The head is turned away and draped for hours: agree tube fixation and the no-relaxant plan at the same conversation.
Shave a narrow strip behind the ear if needed; keep the pinna and face exposed under a clear drape.
Otological objective; position for both the mastoid and the canal views.
Postaural and canal infiltration. Infiltration near the stylomastoid foramen can cause a temporary facial weakness; note it for the recovery check.
In acute mastoiditis, a subperiosteal abscess is opened and pus sent before the cortex is drilled.
Bone wax for bleeding bone and emissary veins; never diathermy on the sigmoid sinus.
Cholesteatoma matrix and any granulations to histology; pus to microbiology in acute disease.
Layered closure of the musculoperiosteal flap and skin, ear pack in the canal, and a mastoid head bandage.
Record which landmarks were identified, the state of the ossicles and any fistula or dehiscence, and the plan for second look or surveillance.

step.mastoid.cortical.title: Cortical mastoidectomy: tegmen, sigmoid, antrum, lateral canal
step.mastoid.cortical.why: Every mastoid operation starts here, and the order matters. Finding the tegmen and sigmoid first defines the safe box; finding the antrum and the lateral semicircular canal then places the facial nerve before any work is done near it.
how: With a large cutting burr, drill a triangle bounded by the temporal line above, a line just behind the posterior canal wall in front, and the mastoid tip below, saucerising as you go deeper.
Identify the tegmen by its colour and the change in bone texture, and follow it backwards. Identify the sigmoid sinus plate posteriorly. Thin both, do not expose them.
Go deeper parallel to the posterior canal wall, keeping it thin but intact, towards the antrum. Recognise and drill through Koerner's septum if present.
Enter the antrum and identify the lateral semicircular canal in its floor with a diamond burr. State aloud that it has been identified.
In acute mastoiditis, remove pus and diseased air cells, open the antrum widely and confirm the aditus is patent. That may be the whole operation.
pitfalls: Starting too far anteriorly and drilling into the canal or towards the facial nerve.
Drilling on a cell track inferiorly before the antrum is found, following disease rather than landmarks.

step.mastoid.canal-wall-down.title: Take the posterior canal wall down to the facial ridge
step.mastoid.canal-wall-down.why: A canal wall down operation turns the mastoid, attic and canal into one cavity that can be inspected for life. The cavity heals well only if the facial ridge is low and smooth, and lowering it is where the facial nerve is most at risk.
how: Open the attic by removing the bone of the scutum and lateral attic wall, protecting the ossicles, and follow disease forwards.
Remove the posterior bony canal wall progressively, with a large burr laterally and a diamond burr medially, keeping the canal skin elevated and protected.
Lower the facial ridge towards the level of the nerve, drilling parallel to its course from the second genu down, with irrigation. Use the lateral canal and the stimulator to confirm position.
Remove the anterior buttress and the bridge, and smooth the cavity so there is no overhang or sump where debris will collect.
structuresAtRisk: Facial nerve, mastoid segment and second genu
pitfalls: A high facial ridge left because of fear of the nerve, giving a discharging cavity. Lower it under control instead.
Drilling perpendicular to the nerve across the ridge.

step.mastoid.disease-clearance.title: Clear cholesteatoma and assess the ossicles
step.mastoid.disease-clearance.why: Residual matrix becomes recurrent disease, but matrix stripped off the stapes footplate or a fistula can cost the patient their hearing and balance. Removing it is a balance of completeness and safety that is decided structure by structure.
how: Lift the matrix in one sheet where possible, working from known anatomy towards the disease, with gentle suction and a moist cottonoid.

Assess the ossicles: check the incus, the incudostapedial joint, the stapes superstructure and mobility. Separate the incudostapedial joint before working on the incus or malleus near an intact stapes.
Inspect the lateral semicircular canal for an erosion. If a fistula is found, do not suction over it; leave matrix on it or remove it last with senior input, and cover it immediately with fascia.
Use an angled endoscope to check the sinus tympani, facial recess and anterior epitympanum for residual disease.
Remove an eroded incus or malleus head if it is involved. Record what remains of the chain.
pitfalls: Pulling matrix off the stapes and opening the vestibule.
Assuming the facial canal is intact: dehiscence of the tympanic segment is common and the nerve may lie under the matrix.

step.mastoid.complication-bailout.title: Bail-out: sinus bleeding, dural exposure, facial nerve injury or fistula
step.mastoid.complication-bailout.why: Each of these is survivable when recognised and handled calmly at the time, and dangerous when it is hidden or chased with the drill. Stop, control, call for help, and record.
how: Sigmoid sinus bleeding: press with a cottonoid and oxidised cellulose or gelatin sponge, tilt the head up only modestly, and tell the anaesthetist because of the risk of air embolism. Do not diathermy the sinus or pack it so tightly that it thromboses into the jugular system.
Dural exposure or cerebrospinal fluid leak: stop drilling there. Repair a leak with fascia or a multilayer graft; a dural tear with brain herniation needs senior or neurosurgical help.

Facial nerve: if the monitor fires repeatedly or the nerve is seen injured, stop and call the consultant. Record the site and extent. A partial injury involving a large part of the nerve or a transection needs repair or grafting, often at the same sitting.
Unexpected extensive disease, a dead ear risk, or loss of landmarks: it is acceptable to stage the operation and finish another day.
pitfalls: Packing sigmoid sinus bleeding with so much material that it propagates thrombosis.
A recognised facial nerve injury that is not documented or communicated, then presents as an unexplained palsy the next morning.

step.mastoid.graft-meatoplasty.title: Graft the middle ear and make an adequate meatoplasty
step.mastoid.graft-meatoplasty.why: In a canal wall down operation, a graft rebuilds a closed, aerated middle ear for hearing, and the meatoplasty decides whether the cavity can be seen and cleaned for the rest of the patient's life.
how: Place gelatin sponge in the middle ear for support, then lay temporalis fascia over the stapes head or footplate and on to the facial ridge, or over an ossicular reconstruction if one is used.
Replace the canal skin over the facial ridge and cavity edges where possible.

Make the meatoplasty by excising conchal cartilage behind the meatus and incising the conchal skin into flaps, sutured back, so the meatus will remain large after healing. Its size should match the cavity.
Pack the cavity and canal according to the surgeon's preference, with the meatus opened by the pack.
pitfalls: A meatoplasty that looks generous in theatre but is too small after healing.
Exposing conchal cartilage, which predisposes to perichondritis.
